analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare directly negotiate prescription drug prices with manufacturers, with automatic price caps if talks fail.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2019 by Sen. Bernie Sanders with 8 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, dying in the Senate Finance Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law bans Medicare from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill would repeal that ban and require the government to negotiate prices for the most expensive and most-used Part D drugs. If negotiations failed, the price would automatically be set to the lowest of several benchmarks, including the average price charged in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan. It would also require drug makers to pay Medicare rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income beneficiaries.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in Medicare Part D prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans, who would see lower negotiated prices; low-income beneficiaries would gain an additional rebate mechanism. Taxpayers also benefit because Medicare pays a large share of drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision that forbids the government from negotiating Part D drug prices or setting a formulary, and instead requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices for covered drugs [S2][S3].

Prioritizes negotiation of the 40 most expensive Part D drugs, drugs costing individual beneficiaries over $10,000 a year, drugs with the fastest price increases, and single-source drugs with no cheaper alternative [S3].

If negotiation fails, the price is automatically set to the lowest of the Veterans Affairs contract price, the average manufacturer price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan, or the Medicaid 'best price' [S3].

Requires manufacturers to pay Medicare rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income beneficiaries, with civil penalties on plans that fail to report the information needed to calculate the rebates [S2][S3].
Requires annual public reports on negotiation outcomes and a Government Accountability Office review by the end of 2024 of whether negotiations are actually lowering prices and who benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would earn less from Medicare sales through negotiated prices, international reference-price fallbacks, and new low-income rebates. Drug plans would bear new reporting duties and penalties for late or false reporting.

drawbacks.text: Drug manufacturers and many economists argue that government-set prices tied to foreign price benchmarks, as the fallback in this bill does, could reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines [S3].
The bill lets the Secretary require changes to plan formularies, which would reduce the flexibility private drug plans currently have to design their own formularies and cost-sharing tiers [S3].
The fallback price mechanism is effectively a price cap, and critics argue that legislated caps, rather than true bargaining, can produce arbitrary results for complex biologics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries, the upside is concrete: lower prices on the drugs that drive the most spending, and a floor price tied to what other developed countries pay. The main cost is borne by drug manufacturers, and the strongest honest objection is the risk of slower development of future drugs. Because the bill targets the highest-cost drugs first and requires public reporting on results, its design allows Congress to evaluate that trade-off over time rather than guessing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Act on January 10, 2019, joined by eight Senate Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill received no further action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed in place for the entire Congress, and the rebates and fallback price caps this bill would have imposed were never enacted.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders, no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in a Republican-controlled committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill repeals the ban on Medicare negotiation, forces negotiations on the 40 most costly Part D drugs, and sets a fallback price pegged to foreign prices and Medicaid best price when talks fail. Manufacturers would also owe new rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Plans would have to use a government-negotiated price framework and file detailed reporting with penalties for late or false filings, but they keep the flexibility to negotiate even deeper discounts and preferred formulary placement. Consumers' interest in lower drug costs runs through these plans' operations.

Today, private intermediaries negotiate drug prices on behalf of Part D plans; the bill shifts that negotiating power to the government, reducing the intermediaries' central role, while plans remain free to seek further discounts on top of the negotiated price.
